content: Updog syndrome was a disease that emerged in the 21st century, primarily affecting humans. It was caused by a pathogen known as the SuperBug, whose origins remain controversial. Some theories suggest it may have been developed by an alien species. The syndrome presented with a wide range of symptoms, including inattentiveness, reduced cognitive function, excessive drooling, lethargy interspersed with sudden bursts of activity, uncontrollable diarrhea, compulsive tweeting, and an increased craving for gluten-free products. Despite numerous treatment attempts, the disease was only eradicated in 2069 through a controversial initiative led by Emperor Joffrey. This involved isolating all infected individuals, placing them in cages, and launching them into the sun aboard rockets. This operation, known as Project Best Summer Tan, was funded by trillionaire Jelon Mezos, the first human fusion individual. The syndrome was first documented in 2041 by an American social media influencer, @Kute_Lash_Curls854873, during her coverage of the 14th Burning Fyre Man Fest in northeastern Venezuela. Following this, outbreaks were reported globally. In 2044, the North Korean CDC identified the causative agent as an unusual spherical bacterium with an opaque surface, naming it the SuperBug. The pathogenesis of Updog syndrome involved the SuperBug entering the host through a laser-induced skin breach, following local anesthesia delivered via a Tranq-Dart. The pathogen then migrated to the brain either by traveling through the bloodstream and crossing the blood-brain barrier using its laser beam on a different setting or via teleportation, typically targeting the left lateral ventricle. Once in the brain, the SuperBug established connections with neurons, particularly favoring the corpus callosum, likely due to its access to both hemispheres of the brain. Updog syndrome was highly contagious, with transmission occurring after as little as five seconds of exposure to an infected individual, leading to the so-called 5-second rule. The disease affected all demographics indiscriminately, regardless of age, race, gender, or other factors. Early studies in the 2040s suggested that Updog syndrome might be an exaggerated form of social media addiction. However, these theories were debunked with the advent of the Laser-Pointer-in-Eye diagnostic test, which provided definitive evidence of the disease's biological basis. The only confirmed risk factor for Updog syndrome was prolonged exposure to an infected individual. However, in 2045, the American CDC issued a warning about potential increased susceptibility in certain populations, though these risk factors were not elaborated upon. Screening for Updog syndrome evolved over time. Until 2058, the primary diagnostic tool was the Glowing 1000-Degree Knife Challenge Test. This involved heating a knife to approximately 350 degrees Celsius until it glowed red and presenting it to the suspected patient via a robot. The patient was required to lick the knife three times. A lack of burns indicated a negative result, while sustaining burns confirmed infection. Refusal to participate was also considered a positive result. Both infected patients and the robot were subsequently crushed and incinerated. This method was later replaced by the Laser-Pointer-in-Eye test, introduced in 2058, which was more cost-effective and reusable. This test involved fixing the patient’s head, sewing their eyelids open, and directing a laser pointer at their pupils. Positive results were indicated by screaming, cursing, or involuntary urination. The natural history of Updog syndrome was highly variable. Symptoms could appear within minutes of exposure, though some cases reported delayed onset of up to 54 weeks. Early symptoms included drowsiness, laughter, and a twinkle in the eye. Progression to severe symptoms, such as compulsive tweeting, could occur within 30 minutes to several months. Before the introduction of treatment in 2063, the prognosis was poor, with most patients succumbing within three years. The introduction of Red Kryptonite Crystal (RKC) treatment slightly improved outcomes, but its high cost limited accessibility to only the wealthiest individuals. In 2067, the MRTHA (Martha-Related sTopping Hallucinations Auditory) test-treatment was developed. This involved violently shaking the patient while repeatedly yelling SAVE MARTHA. This method was both diagnostic and therapeutic, often halting or reversing symptom progression. Treated patients were placed in solitary maximum-security quarantines to prevent reinfection and were later included in the Best Summer Tan project. By the end of the project in 2069, the remaining human population, numbering fewer than 5,000, resided in luxurious underground bunkers beneath Mount Rushmore. These facilities featured advanced ventilation systems drawing air from openings in President Lincoln's nose. However, this population was ultimately wiped out when Thor accidentally dropped his hammer on the ventilation hatch and, due to intoxication, forgot its location.
